criterion_notes.c1: The essay discusses household and community water and sanitation service access, particularly municipal water disconnections, free basic water lifeline supplies, prepaid water meters, rural water schemes, and pit-latrine installation in South Africa alongside global debates.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording: Yes — discusses legal, administrative, institutional, and governance debates over water commodification, privatization/public-private partnerships, municipal tariffs, credit control, and the constitutional right to water. Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Yes — discusses rule-type mechanisms directly governing household service access, including tariff and cost-recovery rules (the 6,000 liters/household/month free lifeline block with steep convex upper tariff blocks, $100 co-payments for pit latrines, prepaid water meters, and disconnection enforcement) and municipal utility privatization contracts. Both readings of Criterion 2 are satisfied; exclusion is due to Criterion 3 (E05).
criterion_notes.c3: No — published explicitly as an 'ESSAY' and described in its conclusion as a 'review of the discourses surrounding global and local water apartheid,' the paper is a political-economy and policy commentary narrating debates from the 2002 Johannesburg WSSD, 2003 Kyoto World Water Forum, and 2003 Cancun WTO ministerial. It contains no empirical research design, methods section, sampling frame, or systematic empirical synthesis, relying on speeches, press statements, media reports, a summary table of activist grievances/demands (with only a brief footnote noting August 2002 interviews with Caucus members and no methodological details), and passing citation of secondary national disconnection figures. Excluded as E05.
criterion_notes.c4: Discusses relevant service access outcomes—including municipal water disconnections (citing secondary Project Viability and HSRC figures), unaffordability, self-disconnection under prepaid meters, and low pit-latrine uptake—but only as secondary/anecdotal points within a policy commentary rather than outcomes measured in an empirical study.
criterion_notes.c5: No — because the article is a non-empirical policy and discourse essay, there is no identifiable empirical study design, analytical sample, or structured unit of analysis linking an exposure to an outcome.
criterion_notes.c6: Yes — full text is in English.

study_design: Essay / narrative policy and discourse commentary (no empirical study design reported)
country: South Africa and global / multi-country (narrative discussion of Johannesburg, Kyoto, Cancun, Evian, and Third World privatization sites)
exposure: Water commodification, municipal water privatization/public-private partnerships, convex block tariffs, pit-latrine co-payments, pre-paid water meters, and disconnection credit-control policies (discussed narratively)
outcome: Household water disconnections, unaffordability, and water/sanitation service access (discussed via secondary reports and media accounts)
rationale: Excluded under E05 (No empirical evidence). Although the article addresses household water and sanitation access (c1) and rule-type pricing/cost-recovery and privatization mechanisms (tariff blocks, pit-latrine co-payments, prepaid meters, disconnections; c2 under both plain and narrow readings), it is explicitly an essay ('ESSAY', PDF Page 3) offering a narrative political-economy commentary and discourse review of international water summits and South African water policy debates without an empirical study design, primary data analysis, or systematic empirical synthesis (c3=no, c5=no).
